Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to rise today pursuant to Standing Order 36 to present a petition signed by 250 residents from Thunder Bay, Nipigon, Red Rock, Beard-more, Dorion and Pass Lake.
They are concerned that this Government is planning to automate the lighthouse at Lamb Island on Lake Superior. The lighthouse keeper serves many vital functions and should not be removed.
An automated system cannot respond to distress calls from the many commercial fishermen who use these waters. It cannot prevent incidents of costly violence and theft, nor can it respond quickly to a malfunctioning of the light which is so important to the safety of these fishermen.
The petitioners thus call upon Parliament to order the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) to ensure that the lighthouse keeper be maintained in his position on Lamb Island.

Mr. Speaker, I also want to present a petition prepared and signed by 1,414 Canadians concerning the possible extradition of criminals now in Canadian prisons. We know that these criminals might have, or have allegedly, committed crimes in other countries as well and they should be prosecuted by the authorities of those countries; however, because of some of our laws, these criminals are beyond the reach of other countries.

1. There are 22 PCB waste storage sites (3 federal, 19 private) in the constituency of Kamloops.
(a) The proper safeguards for these wastes are contained in the CEPA Storage of PCB Wastes Interim Order issued on September 22, 1988. The federal government is in the process of leasing two mobile or transportable incinerators for eliminating federal PCB wastes. Mr. Speaker, I have a brief point of order. I believe that earlier this morning we made a tentative arrangement whereby we would divide up the time in a way similar to what we did on Monday night. Perhaps it escaped all of us that at that particular time on Monday night, because it was an adjournment debate, there was no such thing as a question and answer period after the speeches.
I would like to suggest to my colleagues in the other Parties that we should proceed in the following way; that in each round the Party in question decides whether they will have a 20-minute speech, followed by a 10-minute question and answer period. Alternatively, there could be a 10-minute speech, followed immediately by a five-minute question and answer period, followed again by a subsequent 10-minute speech and another five-minute question and answer period. In this way, we will not lose the opportunity to have questions and answers, but we will pro-rate them depending on the length of the speech. In other words, a 20-minute speech will have a 10-minute question and answer period and alternatively, a 10-minute speech will have a five-minute question and answer period.
I have had some discussions with my colleague from the New Democratic Party on this subject. I would like to offer that as a suggestion to the Whip of the Government to see if it has their agreement as well.
I think that we have perhaps inadvertently forgotten that part of the equation in the earlier discussions this morning.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order with respect to the wording of the motion today. I want to try to do it in a spirit of co-operation, trying to be helpful first to the Chair and then to all colleagues of opposition Parties. I will try to make my points as succinctly as possible so as not to take up the precious time of the House, especially considering the nature of the substance of the motion which I think we all agree is a very important issue for all sides of the House.
My point is procedural. It has to do with the wording in the first paragraph of the motion which states, "-that it be an Order of the House that:" followed by the other paragraphs of the motion.
My basis concern is with the phrase: "That it be an Order of the House that:". The problem is that we know of no tradition of Parliament whereby this type of motion, if passed, because of its wording using a phrase
June 8, 1989

like this, ipso facto becomes an order to the Government to introduce specific legislation, to table policy, or to do other things.
According to our knowledge and our research, the ancient and valid tradition, of course, is that Parliament recognizes in its forms and words the difference between a motion which, if agreed, becomes a resolved resolution and, by distinction, a motion which, if agreed, becomes an order.
To put it precisely the House expresses itself to the Government by "resolution" as distinct from an "order" that is given to execute a decision of the House or an order given to different officers of the House in the view of executing that decision.
To support our argument we wish to cite the 1970 edition of the parliamentary dictionary by Abraham and Hawtrey, page 185 where it is stated under the word "Resolution":
An expression of the opinion of the House with reference to some subject or a declaration of its intention to do something. A resolution is sometimes ordered to be communicated to the other House with a request for its concurrence, e.g. a resolution that it is expedient that a joint committee be appointed to consider a certain subject. A resolution may be rescinded.
Resolutions must be distinguished from Orders, i.e. directions or commands addressed by one or other House to members or officers of that House or to other persons. Thus the House of Commons resolves that an address be presented to the Queen, but orders it to be presented to her by those Members who are privy counsellors or members of the royal household.
In light of that argument, we submit the proper way of wording the motion would be, as has always or long been our practice, not to say, "it be an order of the House that-" but instead say, "this House calls on the Government to-". That is the wording which we respectfully submit should be included in this motion.
Having made that point, I want to reiterate to colleagues of opposition Parties that, consistent with Citation 480 of Beauchesne's, we certainly do not expect the Chair to come back immediately with a ruling on the arguments I have just presented. Consistent with the practice of the House, we should get under way the debate of the very important issue that is put before us today.
In that light I think it is reasonable and important for us to obtain a ruling from the Chair so that in the future we can know what to expect. This would reasonably give
Supply
us a good idea of a distinction between the use of one set of words or another set of words.
I humbly suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that in the meantime while Your Honour is reflecting on this matter that perhaps you. Sir, could indicate the different circumstances, if any, which allow or require the use of the phrase: "It be an Order of the House-" such as is used in both Notices of Motions under Private Members' Business in the name of the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the Hon. Member for Kamloops (Mr. Riis) with respect to calling individuals to the bar of the House. I think that is a good example of something the Chair may wish to clear up.
Our basic point is that the use of the words that are proposed to us today would break some new ground. In that context we feel compelled to bring Your Honour's attention to this matter so that it may be clarified and that in the future we know exactly what to expect.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the interjection by my hon. friend and colleague, the Deputy House Leader for the Government, on this issue. I want to explain the reason that these particular words were chosen. I see this issue as different from most issues brought forward on opposition days. I think it is fair to say that on most opposition days the Opposition brings forward a motion which the Government tends not to support. A motion is often aimed in a rather critical way at the Government and, of course, a votable motion normally is actually even designed that way.

Second, who would not say that it was appropriate to have plans in place for the disposal of toxic wastes and so on?

speechtext: I thank the Members. I do not think that was the intention of the Deputy Government House Leader when he made his proposal this morning. We will start the debate immediately with the Hon. Member for Saanich-Gulf Islands

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be addressing the House today during Environment Week. It is a shame that there has been such a delay in the debate which has forced the school children, who were here to observe the beginning of it, to leave.
The Government has endorsed the recommendations of the Brundtland Commission. It has failed, however, to demonstrate a willingness to go beyond rhetoric and deliver the substantive changes necessary. Decisive political action is required now. The motion before the House is an humble attempt to begin that process.
Yesterday in the House the Prime Minister responded to a question from the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan about economic decisions and the environmental assessments connected to them. In June 1988 the Prime Minister said: "We have established mechanisms to ensure that economic decisions take environmental impact into account". He was asked whether the cuts to VIA Rail had been considered in this context. The Prime Minister was very concise. He answered: "No". The beginning of this motion addresses the requirement for environmental assessment. As I stand today in the House I want to tell Members opposite that they must make a fundamental change in their thinking about what is required, if we are to make the changes necessary and solve the real environmental problems in our country.
Supply
Another example of the kinds of contradiction that are myriad within government policy is the fact that the Government is still giving our tax money to the oil companies. For example, in Alberta there is $1 billion for the Hibernia oil field, $650 million for the OSLO tar sands plant, and $325 million for the Lloydminster heavy oil upgrader. This is in the context of being told over and over again that we must reduce our dependency on fossil fuels and that the effects of global warming are so extreme it puts all human life at risk.
In the same context we have cuts to conservation and alternative energy programs. Conservation and renewable energy funding has declined from $400 million per year between 1980 and 1984 to a paltry $49 million for 1989-1990. This is from the post budget departmental briefing estimates.
When we talk about environmental assessment, we also must consider the larger picture of over-all government policies: why the Government is giving money to one portion of the energy sector and taking it away from the kind of conservation and renewable energy sources so necessary to form real alternatives.
The information we have before us on the effects of global warming is most frightening. In the environment committee we heard reports from Jim McNeill, the former Executive Director of the Brundtland Commission. He talked movingly about the testimony of the President of the Maldives, an island nation, before the Brundtland Commission, that if global warming continues at the same rate, that country whose highest elevation is 1.5 metres above sea level-that is about five feet-will disappear beneath the waves in 40 to 60 years.
When we think in those terms and see that our Government is still using our tax dollars to fund fossil fuels, we wonder where the sense of it all is. Global warming will cause a phenomenon that we have not yet experienced, a phenomenon of environmental refugees on a scale unheard of to date. We are talking about multi-millions of people trying to get to higher levels because the oceans will make their homelands disappear.

June 8, 1989
Supply
At a time when we have the contradiction of the Government funding megaprojects, it is crucial for the House to understand that we want environmental assessments of a non-partisan nature but of a crucially political nature. As the Member opposite pointed out, this is the House of Commons. It is a political body. It does not necessarily have to be a partisan body on this issue. We must think in the long term and not the short term, not respond to government polls but respond to the very real and sincere concerns of not only Canadians but of citizens of the world.
We are concerned about the transition to a sustainable society, and the questions arising from that are undeniably large ones.
Fundamental changes are required in the way we weigh costs and benefits and make decisions. The federal Government must be prepared to demonstrate leadership in adopting these changes, not just in matters of national policy but its own day to day operation. In this spirit, this is why we want an environmental officer of the House.
Parliament Hill, as those of us who are new here perhaps see more clearly, is a city within a city. We have an opportunity to demonstrate to Canada and to the world that we are serious about this environmental concern by getting our own house in order and by recycling the paper used here. I come from the Province of British Columbia where we had over the centuries complete destruction of forests. It is not necessary if we recycle wisely.
Implementing the Brundtland report entails more than just mouthing the words of sustainable development and attaching environmentally friendly stickers to everything in sight.
The report envisaged a whole new approach to economic development. We could begin here on Parliament Hill in some of the things that we are doing. We do not just want to tinker at the edges. We must show that we are prepared to undertake fundamental change.
In environmental assessment, we are asking the federal Government to begin an immediate re-evaluation of all its policies and programs asking if each is environmentally sound.
That brings us to my area of interest, that is, international development. In the last Budget, it was clearly demonstrated by the Government that it did not understand the recommendations of the Brundtland Commission or its concern and observation that not only are we interconnected internationally but we are interlocked. We are interdependent. We in a developed country seem to think we are immune from the kind of damage that is occurring internationally in the Third World. The Government felt that immunity sufficient to be able to bring the budget cuts to foreign aid.
What that means is we may reduce our deficit. We are looking after ourselves, but we are exporting the environmental degradation to those countries that can least afford it, those people who are the most vulnerable.
It makes no sense if we place that on a large international scale. Many scientists and other esteemed people have told us that we are on this planet together; if we violate one part of it, all of it is violated. It is the budget proposals on foreign aid, reductions to foreign aid, that demonstrate that the Government has no understanding of that dynamic at all.
As to the concerns about waste products and use of toxic waste, we have a priority substances list under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. There is a need to ensure, however, that time lines for elimination are set. There is a need for targets and timetables for reduction of chemicals in our environment. We must see sustainable development distinct from cleaning up the mess that we are already in. Some 10 per cent of world trade is now in chemicals. They move into the environment. Many work their way up through the food chain to plants, animals, and humans.
Much of our drinking water has been contaminated by toxic substances such as PCBs, dioxins, and furans.
The recent revelation of high PCB levels in the breast milk of Inuit women substantiates the need for national and global action, for zero discharge standards, to prevent pesticides and other potentially harmful chemicals from moving through the atmosphere to be deposited in areas far from their application, storage, or disposal.
With some 100,000 chemicals on the market and some
600,000	new chemicals coming on to the market per year, it is clear that workers and the public are best protected by prohibiting contact in as many locations as possible. It

June 8, 1989
is also increasingly important that producers be required to determine a method of safe disposal of chemicals prior to marketing.
I am quoting from a report just released this week, Towards a Sustainable Future. I was fortunate to be one of five New Democrat Members on a task force that travelled across Canada. This is our offering to the House, Towards a Sustainable Future. I recommend it as reading for all Members of this House, because it is our sincere hope that they will educate themselves about the crucial issues confronting us. As legislators we talk a lot about sustainable development and concern for the environment, but in this place we have a responsibility to act and to legislate. It is not good enough to talk. People have a great deal of disrespect for politicians, and the reason is that they think we are all talk and no action. As the Member for Saanich-Gulf Islands I have no intention of falling into that category.
I want to talk about the concern for water resources, both the fresh water and ocean resources of our country. We have concerns about the dumping that is going on, and the "solution to pollution is dilution" type of thinking that we can no longer afford.
In my province where the pulp and paper industry is large pollution is rampant. We have legislation but no enforcement. We must have enforcement and the powers of our federal Government to come down on those polluters and say "no more" in the interests of Canadians.
We must establish a super fund for cleaning up our environment, in the same manner as the United States. We must come up with a funding mechanism to clean up toxic waste. The U.S. effort to clean up its own environment has been to the detriment of our environment. Recent figures confirm that more that 170,000 tonnes per year of toxic and hazardous waste are presently entering Canada from the United States. Its solution is to export pollution. That is not acceptable. We have a responsibility to clean up our own house, but the United States also has a responsibility to look after its.
We must have a national recycling program. We must have taxes on polluting products, on excess packaging,
Supply
and on packaging that is not recyclable. We have to make it economically unviable to degrade our environment. There are many things that we have to do.
An Environment Canada report recently leaked to Greenpeace indicates that pulp and paper mills are responsible for at least 50 per cent of all water pollution in Canada. That is staggering when one considers the bottom line that those companies use as their determining factor in action. Those people are polluting our environment in order that they can profit from it. Once again, we should be making sure that it is not economically viable to degrade our environment. We should also be giving economic incentives for clean activities.
Finally, I want to talk about oil tanker traffic on the West Coast. As one of the Members representing Vancouver Island, I was intimately connected with the oil spill that occurred off our coast in January. That has brought about many cries for a full public inquiry, not only from Members in the House but from many citizens with high profiles. I know that the Minister of the Environment has met with many of those people. In committee he assured me that there would be a public inquiry. I want to make it clear that what we are asking for, and what they are asking for, is a full public inquiry under the Inquiries Act in order that people can be subpoenaed and we can hear the full story on what happened in that oil spill. We can also look into the exploration of oil in order that we can be more informed about our ocean.
Recently I heard that there has been a fifteenfold increase in barge and crude oil exports out of the Port of Vancouver. As the Member for Saanich-Gulf Islands, as the name implies, the Gulf Islands are in my riding and this is of deep personal concern. Those ships and barges go right by the beautiful Gulf Islands on their way down to Cherry Point, Washington where the oil refinery is. With a fifteenfold increase over five years we certainly have to think of the time bomb ticking and how long we have before the beaches of my riding are befouled by oil. That is why it is crucial that a full public inquiry under the Inquiries Act be implemented. We have to answer those questions about long-term planning to prevent the befoulment of beaches of the Pacific Rim National Park.

June 8. 1989
Supply
This motion is put forth as an humble attempt to address the sustainable development agenda of the House. The clock is ticking and we are running out of time. There is an urgency, and the public is aware of the urgency. I think the public is way ahead of us in its thinking. Politicians who do not listen to the public are not politicians for very long. We must address this issue. We have to be courageous with the type of decisions that we have to make. We have to put aside partisan interests and stop trying to make political points on one another. We have to change. We as human beings do not like to change. It is a scary thing to change, but it is necessary, or we are all doomed. On that light note I will bring my remarks to a conclusion.

I listened with interest to the comments of the Hon. Member for Saanich-Gulf Islands. I would like to make a brief comment and also ask a question.
I am fortunate to come from an area in rural Manitoba where we have clean air and clean water. The people I represent have come to realize, as have all Canadians, that the number one issue that we are facing as Canadians and as residents of the planet earth is the protection and preservation of our environment. I believe that it will be the number one issue in the future, starting now, as a matter of fact.
The Hon. Member talked about going beyond rhetoric and the fact that politicians cannot only talk about environmental concerns, that there has to be action. I have to take the Hon. Member to task on that comment, because there has been talk from this Government and also action. There was a federal environmental assessment and review process on the Sea Island fuel barge facility where it was concluded by the panel that the Minister of Transport unconditionally rejected the proposal submitted by the North Fraser Harbour Commission. That is an example of where the federal Government has taken action.
Up until the spring of 1988 Manitoba had an NDP Government. We had a perfect example with the NDP Government in Manitoba of all talk and no action. A group of environmental organizations did an assessment, province by province, of all the provincial Governments in late 1987 or early 1988. The New Democratic Government in Manitoba ranked dead last. That is a perfect
example of a Government that was all talk and no action. I have a question I would like to ask. I do not think that there is any Member in this House that would disagree with the fact that we have to develop alternate sources of energy.
The Hon. Member mentioned in her remarks that there is a contradiction in spending the money that is being spent on the fossil fuel megaprojects. I would like to ask the Member what we as a nation would do if we did not invest in the megaprojects and there was a time gap between a future serious fuel shortage and the development of a viable alternate source of energy? What would we as Canadians do if we were faced with a time gap if we quit investing in the fossil fuel megaprojects?

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the question and applaud the Member in a spirit of non-partisanship for any action that the Government takes on reducing the damage to our environment. I welcome the example that he has given to this House.
Addressing his question about the time lag, I realize that we have to wean ourselves away from fossil fuels. We cannot do it overnight. The examples I have of program cuts illustrate that at the time we are giving money to subsidize those megaprojects, there have been cuts to the programs such as Canada Oil Substitution Program, that went in 1986, the Canadian Home Insulation Program, that went in 1986, the Canadian Energy Audit Program, that went in 1986, the Atlantic Energy Conservation Investment Program, that went in 1986, the Solar Energy Demonstration Program, that was gone in 1989, the Remote Community Demonstration Program, that went in 1989, the Forest Industry Renewable Energy Program, that was gone in 1989, Industrial Conversion Assistance Program, that went in 1987.
So my answer is that we have to change our thinking. I realize that a weaning away process is necessary but we also have to start funding other types of program so that real alternatives are viable.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to indicate to the House my pleasure in having an opportunity to address this very important issue. I would like to thank the Hon. Member for the motion she has presented today and for the spirit in which it is presented.
June 8, 1989

I would also like to state to Members of the House that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) regrets that he cannot be present at this time, but will be returning shortly to the House from Montreal. As Members may know, the Minister is in Montreal this morning announcing details, in co-operation with the Province of Quebec, of the implementation of the St. Lawrence Action Plan. I think all of us who are aware of the deterioration which has taken place in the quality of the St. Lawrence will welcome this initiative on behalf of the federal and Quebec governments.
As Members of this House also know, this Government and this Minister have given a very strong commitment both in our actions and in the Throne Speech, to the environment in general and in particular in the Throne Speech, to the need to introduce legislation in the House for the environmental assessment of its activities. I can assure the Members of the House that officials at this very moment are preparing the necessary documentation for the introduction of that legislation to the House.
I think that at the outset of a debate of this importance, it is necessary to establish some sort of groundwork or framework in which to judge what is being done, what has been done in the past and what is needed for the future. It is important to the Members of this House and for the public to have a clear awareness of the way in which Government goes about the process of assessment of environmental effects of its activities.
There has been a process of environmental assessment in place since 1974. That initial process, started by the Liberal Government of that day, contained a rather loosely worded cabinet directive which placed a great deal of faith in government's voluntary willingness to do the right thing by the environment. The process at that time did not have a great deal of public credibility. There was not very much progress until the present Speaker of this House, at a time when he had other responsibilities during the Government of 1979-1980, initiated what proved to be time-consuming and complex policy development work including very extensive consultations needed to produce credible legislation in this most important area.
This legislation is absolutely fundamental to having
Supply
environmentally effective Government decision-making.
I believe that this Government and all Members of this House would accept the fact that it is exceedingly important that what be done be done properly and effectively. Many of the principles in the existing process are valid if conscientiously applied. Since returning to office in 1984, this Government has over the past five years paid particular attention to ways of improving the process with respect to day to day practice in advancing towards the stage where we are now, the preparation of environmental assessment legislation.
I would like to explain to the House some of the more important aspects of the way in which environmental assessments are done as of now and some of the principles we would propose to incorporate into the new law as soon as it is available.
The Canadian federal approach is based on a judgment that is shared by most of the industrialized world and I believe to a significant degree by the developing world. That judgment is that environmental impact assessment is an essential element in the applying of economic development initiatives. Such assessments will help avoid potentially serious environmental and related social problems which could greatly reduce the value of apparent economic progress. Good environmental assessments result in good development and makes good economic sense.
The federal environmental assessment and review process, which we know as EARP is an administrative process set out by Order in Council applicable to proposed federal Government initiatives or private sector undertakings for which the federal Government has some decision-making responsibility. Their process is a self-assessment procedure in that the government agency with the main decision-making responsibility in each instance undertakes the preliminary screening and, if needed, the more detailed initial assessment of the proposed activity. However, where in the opinion of that agency there is likely to be significant environmental effects, the project must be referred to the Ministry of the Environment for public review by an independent panel appointed by that Minister.

June 8, 1989
Supply
The Federal Environment Assessment Review Office, known as FEARO, is a small agency which reports directly to the Environment Minister, organizes a review, provides logistic support and often provides a panel chairman. Elistorically, I would note in passing that only a small percentage of the projects undergoing initial assessment have proved to have sufficiently severe environmental effects that they have required the public review of which I am referring.
Upon the completion of this review the panel provides a report to the Minister of the Environment and to the initiating Minister, the Minister responsible for the agency proposing to undertake or authorize a project. This report which is a public report, contains the recommendations of the panel. While these recommendations are not binding, the initiating Minister is expected to outline publicly his or her response to that report. Certainly those recommendations are of monumental significance.
In early 1984 the Federal Environmental Assessment Review Office completed its own review, initiated, as I referred to earlier by the present Speaker in another capacity, of the operation of EARP and made recommendations for improvements to the then Environment Minister.
These recommendations were incorporated in the present guidelines as of June 21, 1984. These guidelines and the Act under which they are operating, the Government Organization Act of 1979, give the Minister of the Environment the responsibility to initiate, recommend and undertake programs of the Government of Canada that are designed:
To ensure that new federal projects, programs and activities are assessed early in the planning process for potential adverse effects of the quality of the natural environment, and that a further review of those projects is carried out of those projects, programs and activities that are found to have probable significant adverse effects, and the results thereof taken into account.
Earlier this year, the Federal Court when rendering a decision on the Rafferty-Alameda project in Saskatchewan determined that the guidelines to which I have now referred are in fact the binding regulation. The main thrust of these guidelines is to require government Departments to conduct their screening and initial assessment activity in a systematic, open and documentable fashion. Detailed instructions to assist Departments in how to do this are provided. The hallmarks are brevity, simplicity, and openness.
It was recognized from the outset that the concerns and responsibilities of the provinces must be taken into account in the operation of the Environmental Assessment Review Panel. Consequently, in regard to any public review, FEARO is required, where needed, to negotiate co-operative federal-provincial or territorial arrangements. Co-operative reviews between jurisdictions are intended to avoid duplication, to reduce costs and to expedite the decision-making process. Most of the public reviews conducted by the Environmental Assessment Review Panels have involved varying degrees of federal-provincial co-operation, ranging from co-chairmanship in some cases, to a case where jointly appointed single chairmen through the appointment of a provincial member to a federal panel. Because of the importance of federal-provincial co-operation in this area, and the realization that such co-operation must continue to exist, it is important to look at a number of examples as to how the process has worked to date.
Several of the reviews are being conducted by panels jointly appointed by federal and provincial Governments and are operating under the terms of reference negotiated between them. Because the reports are purely advisory, they tend to develop without regard to jurisdictional divisions, thus providing a holistic view of the social and environmental impact of a given project.
In fact, some joint environmental reviews, such as West Coast offshore drilling, have been undertaken on proposals where a jurisdictional dispute was still occurring. But that assessment has taken place without prejudice to the final result of that dispute.
The degree of federal or provincial participation in each case has generally reflected the extent to which the major decisions are being made by one or the other government. For example, a panel set up to assess the expansion of the Vancouver airport, which was clearly a federal responsibility but with some impact on provincial responsibilities, is federally chaired and supported but has amongst its members a provincial nominee. At the other end of the spectrum are the panels which assess the Arctic pilot project's southern terminals in Quebec
June 8, 1989

and Nova Scotia. These are provincially chaired and supported but contain federal nominees.
The nuclear generating project in New Brunswick was planned by a joint federal-provincial Crown corporation to be operated by the New Brunswick Power Commission, a provincial utility. Substantial federal financial credits from the federal Government were needed for the project to proceed. Thus, both Governments had major responsibility and it was decided that a fully joint assessment would be most appropriate. In Nova Scotia, the Venture offshore gas development project was conducted in a similar manner.
In 1983 a federal Government-B.C. memorandum of agreement called for a joint federal-provincial review of environmental and related social and economic effects of a renewed program of petroleum exploration off B.C's northern coast. The review was held without prejudice to the ultimate ownership of the resource and managed within the joint framework of the Provincial Environmental Management Act and the federal Management Act and the federal EARP.
In view of the evolving situation in Canada's North, it seems very logical that territorial Governments must be a part of this process in the future. By the same token, the importance of land claims agreements are resulting in larger roles for native communities in managing environmental assessment procedures. EARP's flexibility must be sufficient to accommodate both of these developments.
It is appropriate to note that the guidelines often required federal government agencies to take into account environmental impacts external to Canada. I believe the Hon. Member referred to that.
This is the basic outline of the environmental assessment process as it now exists and how it works in co-operation with the provinces.
Not surprisingly, environmental assessments, whether they be federally, provincially or jointly managed, have over the years given rise to concerns about costs, uncertainty as to data and research requirements, potential regulatory duplication and delays.
Costs affecting the economics of a proposed activity are of concern to all developers. It follows that every effort must be made by administrators to ensure that information requirements and other obligations imposed upon proponents are reasonable and restricted to
Supply
those necessary for the conduct of a responsible and adequate review.
Obviously the collection and the analysis of environmental and related social data and, in the case of formal public reviews, the appointment of a panel and the conduct of hearings carry a cost in both time and money. Such costs must, however, be weighed against the very considerable costs that can be incurred if mitigating measures involving significant redesign have to be introduced after the construction of the project is under way or even completed because of the emergence of an unanticipated environmental damage and a weak or strong public opposition.
Underlying such more obvious costs are the costs in lost opportunities, slowed natural productivity, reduction in environmental sustainability, and even health risks that can result from insensitively designed projects. As a general comment on the costs of environmental assessment, it should be noted that these costs historically average only 0.5 per cent of the capital cost of the project.
It should also be stressed that one of the objectives of the EARP is to facilitate and place in a constructive context public input to government decision-making.
The concerns of society at large must be taken into account when dealing with possible changes in the natural environment. Resource managers, whether they be private or public, are expected to be responsible stewards. People affected by a proposed activity have a right to be heard and in a setting in which they can have a reasonable expectation that there views will be seriously considered. Experience has shown that information derived from such local knowledge is exceedingly valuable in deciding on project design, timing and management. This process, if done correctly, can be considered to be an important and legitimate part of the cost of the entire project and will ultimately contribute to a far better project.
Experience has shown all of us that the technical quality of planning and design has often been enhanced by the demands of a public review, sometimes even to the point that such reviews may well prove cost effective for industry in the longer term, quite apart from their environmental benefits. Moreover, when the results of work under the EARP have been incorporated into project planning and design, proponents have realized that they can proceed with greater confidence about the long-term acceptability of what is proposed. This is reassuring to them, to government and certainly to society in general.

Supply
It is our experience that industry is supportive of environmental assessment activities as long as the information demands are reasonable, duplication is avoided and a clear, timely decision results.
There exists a similar potential for duplication between the EARP and formal regulatory processes within the federal structure.
A notable example is the National Energy Board which, under its enabling legislation, is assigned regulatory powers which include the licensing of the export of oil, gas and electricity, the issuance of certificates of public convenience and necessity for interprovincial and international pipelines and international power lines, and the setting of just and reasonable tolls for pipelines under federal jurisdiction.
Under the board review procedures there is a standing requirement for environmental impact assessment of projects needing board approval. If a given project has also been subject to public review under the EARP, criticism can arise over apparent duplication.
The EARP is most effective when it is used as a planning tool rather than as a regulatory device. Used as a planning tool, it should be brought into play at the earliest possible opportunity to assist in identifying potential environmental problems and to help design solutions for them. Such an approach encourages better project design and allows for the required regulatory activity to occur without duplication but with the benefit of substantive early environmental planning.
Obviously, early application of the EARP, including public reviews as needed, is also the answer to concerns over delays whether or not a formal regulatory process is involved.
It is our experience that well-managed environmental assessment can reduce delays in securing project approvals. Not only can it reduce public conflict about a given project, but early environmental assessments, particularly those involving public reviews, can also cause early project planning to be carried out at an impressive level of detail and quality. This in turn often means that projects are better thought out resulting in fewer and shorter delays during construction and fewer cost overruns. Good environmental assessment is good planning, which is good business.
In closing, I wish to reinforce the importance of legislating this process to ensure that this and future governments are required to assess the environmental effects of our actions. The Canadian public must be assured that potential environmental problems will be caught before they can become significant public problems.
Environmental considerations must be at the heart of our decision-making.
There is a new ethic evolving in Canada which is making environmental considerations a determinant of economic change, rather than the historical pattern, of the economy being a determinant of environmental change. We are all well aware, too much aware in fact, Mr. Speaker, of the problems that result when the latter strategy is in place.
I suggest in closing that what is even more important, however, is to ensure that when the guidelines are brought into legislation, as they will be hopefully in the very near future, that the process is done properly, that the guidelines are properly, adequately structured into law. It is more important that the process be done correctly, than it be done hastily. This issue is too important for mistakes to be made.
We understand that the task before us, the task to which the motion in part refers, is exceedingly important and we give it a very high priority, and agree in principle with the motion that is being presented and debated today.
The Government will be unable to support the motion because of at least in part the inappropriate deadlines which it imposes.
Again, in closing, the task is an important one. I believe there are no partisan differences in the House on that. The need, however, is to ensure that it is done correctly.

When the Free Trade Agreement was being negotiated, the federal Conservatives seemed to see nothing wrong with allowing Americans in to examine the books of Canadian logging companies.
I think that if we look at the non-proliferation treaty, there is a specific initiative in that treaty which permits host countries to make sure that the material they are sending out of a nuclear nature is being properly utilized.
In so far as Congressman Synar's legislation is concerned, I think there could be a bilateral accord. The current bilateral accord is not worth the paper it is written on in so far as the concerns about sovereign use of our own territory are concerned.
Congressman Synar's Bill could be modified and worked upon in a bilateral way between Canada and the United States. The intention of it is to prevent U.S. companies from using other countries, including Canada and Third World countries, as a dumping ground for unwanted American waste. The intention of making sure that the waste is disposed of in a proper fashion is built in to give that assurance. I think we could work out something in a bilateral way which would achieve Congressman Synar's objectives without in any way inhibiting Canadian's right to control and develop our own regulations.

June 8, 1989
I think that the Government's immediate knee-jerk response to try to block the Synar Bill is in fact a response which has been motivated by big business, which has been motivated by two or three Canadian companies that have made multi-millions of dollars in importing hazardous waste. It has very little to do with an intrinsic concern about Canadian sovereignty.
I do not buy the sovereignty argument. It is a red herring. If the Government is truly concerned about dealing with the issue of importing waste from the United States, which is coming in by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes, I think it should support Synar's Bill in principle and work to modify those areas of concern.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, recent decisions by the Government have left the Canadian dairy industry facing a very serious and immediate crisis, and a highly uncertain future.
The cap that has been put on industrial milk prices until December, 1990, while allowing decreases in industrial milk prices if the cost of production formula goes down, has left the dairy farmers of Canada wondering where is that commitment that the Government claims it has to protect the dairy industry?
When is the Government going to stop hammering the dairy farmers' managed supply system, while at the same time claiming commitment to the industry while it watches it disintegrate?

Mr. Speaker, some families in Atlantic Canada are faced with income reductions of 50 per cent or more this year, and the
prospects for the next two years are not much better. Particularly hard hit are young families who, despite significant reduction in income, must still meet mortgage and boat payments. With recent rises in interest rates, those payments certainly have not been reduced, let alone in proportion to income reductions. For those young families, and in some cases those of their parents who have co-signed mortgages, foreclosure would spell disaster.
Canada needs those hard-working young people, economically strong and healthy. During their short-term difficulties they need our help in order that they can contribute to Canada for many years once our fishery recovers.
Accordingly, I urge the Government to establish special support measures to assist those families through their short-term time of difficulty.
If, Mr. Speaker, as you walk through the forest you encounter a fire, you digress from your path to put it out before it spreads. This fire of economic crisis must be put out now.

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF CONSTRUCTION OF TRANSPORT CANADA BUILDING
CANCELLATION OF CONSTRUCTION OF TRANSPORT CANADA BUILDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 9 the Minister of Public of Works (Mr. MacKay) stated in the House that the Government's decision to shelve the construction of a new building for Transport Canada in favour of renewing the Department's lease with Mr. Robert Campeau had "resulted in considerable savings". Similarly, the budget speech of the Minister of Finance refers to the cancellation of a new building as an "expenditure reduction".
Yesterday, in his appearance before the Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Minister of Public Works flatly contradicted his earlier statement and stated that he has no idea if the renewal of Transport Canada's lease with Mr. Campeau will result in any savings, and that it might actually end up costing the taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars.
In a more disturbing admission, the Minister also stated that the decision to shelve a new building in favour of a renewal of the lease was motivated by political and not financial considerations, the decision did not actually have to save money as long as the cancellation of a new building gave the "perception" of belt tightening.
I call upon the Minister to come clean with the Canadian taxpayer and remove the inefficiency and
June 8, 1989

double dealing that has plagued the Transport Canada project from its inception by stating clearly and unequivocally-

Mr. Speaker, this is National Access Awareness Week, and I would like to take this opportunity to remind my colleagues in the House, and all Canadians, of the importance of promoting the full integration of disabled persons into all sectors of Canadian society.
Canada is a country that respects the rights of all people, a country where everyone is encouraged to do his or her best. Yet for disabled Canadians, who represent close to 15 per cent of the population, even simple, every day activities can pose enormous problems.
This week should be an occasion for us to work together to find ways to remove physical and other types of barriers that prevent persons with disabilities from participating fully in Canadian society.
May I congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on the special attention you have personally given to this week, declaring, among other things, yesterday June 7, as Employment Day on the Hill. Further, I commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on the declaration of National Access Awareness Week, as one way to help improve attitudes of Canadians toward their fellow citizens who are disabled.

subtopic: THE CRAB INDUSTRY IN THE ACADIAN PENINSULA
THE CRAB INDUSTRY IN THE ACADIAN PENINSULA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a joint meeting was held on the weekend in the Acadian Peninsula to report on the crisis now raging in the crab industry.
At this meeting, all concerned were able to make recommendations to broaden the economic base of the Acadian Peninsula.
Mr. Speaker, the whole fishing industry of northeastern New Brunswick is going through an extremely difficult period and this industry alone cannot continue to support the region economically.
That is why I ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to mandate the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Valcourt) to set up a task force, together with the Minister of Public Works and Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act (Mr. MacKay) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall), to find solutions to help these courageous and capable workers who now find themselves in an intolerable situation.
Mr. Speaker, the federal Government must deal with this question immediately to show that it understands the frustration of these Acadian workers who are entitled to live and work in respect and dignity.

Mr. Speaker, I draw the attention of Hon. Members to the May 22 issue of Western Report magazine and the growing popularity of Resolution No. 1. Resolution No. 1 states that all future tax increases should be exceeded by expenditure reductions until the Budget is balanced. This is the first sign of a taxpayer backlash to the recent Budget.
The PC Budget does not show restraint. It increases the deficit and it increases spending on an over-bloated public sector. I urge someone, anyone, in the PC Caucus to speak out against this. Where are the fiscal conservatives?
I wish Resolution No. 1 well. Western Canadians have learned that the most effective protest is done at the ballot box. I warn members of the Progressive Conservative Party, continue your tax and spend policies and it is only a matter of time until Tories all across Canada will face a new political option based on free enterprise and fiscal responsibility.

June 8, 1989

subtopic: THE LEAKING OF VISCOUS LIQUID IN SENNETERRE
THE LEAKING OF VISCOUS LIQUID IN SENNETERRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a June 4, 1989 Canadian Press article by Camille Beaulieu is headlined "Viscous liquid leak from American railroad car at Senneterre". He is referring to car No. 524335 which was part of a CN convoy and belongs to an American company, Southern. It has been shunt lined in the Senneterre switching yard because of damage. CN repair work order No. 6229 dated June 2 indicates that "as a result of damage to the car which was side lined at Senneterre for repairs, it was noted that it contained a few copper plates. It is in fact loaded with barrels containing all sorts of unidentified products and the barrels are unsealed. Some of them have been tipped over and liquids seep under the car". This car crossed into Quebec around May 19, 1989, which means that CN management have let this car travel across Quebec cities and villages for a number of days without being concerned about the liquid seeping under the car.
Mr. Speaker, thank God the CN employees at Senneterre are competent and look after the environment in Abitibi!
^

Mr. Speaker, the Budget of the Government has imposed some of the most brutal, callous, and regressive taxes upon Canadians, including a goods and service tax which will even tax the homes that Canadians want to buy.
Officials in the office of the Minister have stated that this tax may be refundable, partially refundable, or not refundable, depending on who one speaks to. Home buyers and home builders deserve to know what is going on in order that they can make their plans.
In addition, the Minister of State for Housing (Mr. Redway) states that the cancellation of the rental RRAP is because this program is not fully targeted to needy Canadians. Nothing can be further from the truth. Housing groups in municipalities across the country disagree. In fact rental RRAP is a program that is very
effective and targeted to those tenants who deserve decent accommodation. The Government should look at the real facts.

Mr. Speaker, June 4 to June 10 is Canadian Environment Week. To mark this important week, I see fit to announce a federal grant of $435,000 to the Centre for Atmospheric Research (CARE), in Egbert, Ontario, to allow the facility to expand.
Construction of the addition to this Centre is under way. The Centre will develop new weather monitoring instruments, as well as research and study climate change on water resources and forests.
CARE is the only research station of its kind in Canada. The Centre is located in a rural environment in Simcoe Centre to ensure that measurements are not affected by the higher air pollution levels usually found in urban areas.
The CARE facility will permit new technology to be developed that will keep Canada at the forefront of environmental, atmospheric research.

subtopic: UPGRADING OF BIG RIVER SUBDIVISION RAIL LINE
UPGRADING OF BIG RIVER SUBDIVISION RAIL LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 13, I attended a meeting of grain producers and concerned citizens in Debden, Saskatchewan where the discussion centred almost entirely on the need for the upgrading of the rail line between Debden and Big River, Saskatchewan.
On June 2, in response to a letter that I sent to him, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard), conceded that the line known as the Big River subdivision had been designated for upgrading in May, 1984. However, immediately following that year's general election, the project was cancelled in September, 1984.
The Minister now states that the early termination of the branch line rehabilitation program, which had enough money in it to complete the Big River subdivision upgrading, has killed the project, and no funding for this line will now be approved.
June 8. 1989

The Minister and the Government are playing with the future of entire communities here, and I call upon the Minister to immediately rethink the elimination of the branch line rehabilitation program, and to honour previously agreed to commitments such as the Big River subdivision.

Mr. Speaker, as a 20 year member of the parliamentary Press Gallery, including several years on a Gallery executive, I am well aware of the hits journalists take from politicians and the public. But they are nothing like the hits that journalists are risking right now in Beijing, Shanghai and elsewhere during this tragedy in China. Our contributing journalists to Canadian newspapers, TV and radio newscasts are witnessing scenes totally beyond human understanding. They are living and reporting a horrible piece of history on the run.
I was moved to hear The Globe and Mail's Jan Wong tell first hand on CBC Morningside:
I saw that young man climbing upon a tank and stopping a whole convoy. It happened right outside my window and I couldn't help crying.
The passing of a brown envelope at a west end Ottawa gas station pales by comparison to the heroism of reporters defying martial law in a country where they beat foreign journalists and shoot at random through windows of diplomatic residences. Vive la presse libre.

subtopic: PHIL LATULIPPE FOUNDATION FOR HANDICAPPED CHILDREN
PHIL LATULIPPE FOUNDATION FOR HANDICAPPED CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Phil Latulippe is an outstanding Canadian who at 70 years of age is running across Canada with the key desire to raise $300,000 for the Phil Latulippe Foundation for recreation programs for handicapped children. As generous Canadians, let us all get behind this remarkable man and his wonderful and dedicated wife, Lucie.
I first met Phil Latulippe when he was a Sergeant in the Canadian Forces and stationed with the Second Field Ambulance at CFB Petawawa. He decided 22 years ago that he was going to stop drinking and smoking and get himself into shape. The base race track was one-half mile long. So he decided to walk it non-stop 365 times, once for each day of the year. It took him nearly two days to walk the 182.5 miles. During that time General S.V. Radley-Walters who was base commander asked me and several others to take turns walking with him to keep up his morale, and we did. The retired Canadian Forces chief warrant officer who used to smoke three packs of cigarettes a day is out to beat his own cross-Canada running record which he set in 1981.
All Canadians wish Phenomenal Phil well and Godspeed. Thank you, Phil, for being such an excellent example to all of us.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF CANADIAN AS SECRETARY GENERAL
APPOINTMENT OF CANADIAN AS SECRETARY GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my great privilege to advise the House that yesterday morning in London, England, the governing body of the International Maritime Organization, a specialized agency of the United Nations, selected William O'Neil as their next Secretary General.
This is the first time that a Canadian has headed a specialized United Nations agency for over 40 years and it is something of which all Canadians should be proud. It reflects Canada's deep commitment and participation in the affairs of IMO since its founding in 1948.
The IMO is committed to enhancing the safety of life at sea and promoting a cleaner marine environment by the prevention of pollution from ships. These admirable objectives are supported by all Canadians. Canada should be proud that these goals will be pursued by a Canadian who has dedicated himself to public service in the marine world for over 40 years.

June 8, 1989
Oral Questions
Mr. William O'Neil was the first Commissioner of the Canadian Coast Guard and for the past 10 years he has been the President of the St. Lawrence Seaway authority. His election as Secretary General reflects highly on his personal credibility in the international maritime circles and also reflects highly on Canada's reputation as a supporter of safer shipping and cleaner oceans.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in response to certain comments the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made to the media yesterday about the refusal of many scientists to relocate with the space agency.
No government would make a decision on health care without consulting the medical profession. No one would consider changes to the court system without consulting the legal profession. This Government has demonstrated that it makes no decisions about business without consulting with business. Why then should the Prime Minister treat with contempt the space scientists who claim only the right to the same consideration?

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister also stated that he is not concerned over the fact that only 4 of the 56 scientists now working in Ottawa are prepared to move to Saint-Lambert and that there are a lot of people who are just waiting to pick up the challenge.

I invite the Prime Minister into the real world, a world where underfunded universities struggle to produce qualified scientists and a world where experienced scientists are so hard to find in this country that they do not have to tolerate the ignorant contempt of opportunistic politicians. There are other places where they can go and where they will go if this Government fails to recognize their voices in decisions affecting them and their families.

Mr. Speaker, the struggle between age and beauty came to a head last night as the MPs took on the Pages in a game of baseball.
For the first time in 11 years, the MPs decided to let the Pages win. The starting pitcher, the Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer), had the Pages trailing 12-2 but then the so-called "terminator" from Bonaventure- Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Gray) let the MP's lead slide and consequently had to take his first loss of the season at 14-13. Lawrence "superpage" Weiner drove in the winning run. Page Petra Kuret slid home to score in the bottom of the ninth.
In total 35 Pages took on a puny squad of 22 overweight, out of shape Members of Parliament. Captain Richard Gabruch masterminded the complex strategy to lead the Pages to a narrow victory. The Member from Lethbridge (Mr. Thacker) summed up the game nicely: "Good guys don't always finish last".

subsubtopic: CALL FOR BAN ON OIL EXPORTS FROM PORT OF VANCOUVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this being International Environment Week and as the Prime Minister is speaking on the environment in Vancouver today, I have questions for the Minister of the Environment.
Following the Gray's Harbour and Exxon Valdez spills, the Minister of the Environment refused our request to have a public examination of the situation. Instead he said he would have a "short, swift and strong" bureaucratic review. He will know that British Columbia's oil spill adviser has now called for a total ban on all exports of oil from the Port of Vancouver. Since he has refused our proposal for a public inquiry and since he is going to review this matter himself, would he now give us the quick answer that he promised us and tell us what his reaction is to the B.C. adviser's proposition to ban all exports from the Port of Vancouver?

subtopic: MEETING WITH CANADIAN FEDERATION OF MUNICIPALITIES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MEETING WITH CANADIAN FEDERATION OF MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is no surprise that the Prime Minister is speaking on the environment at a Tory fundraiser tonight.
He will not be joining myself and other Members of Parliament at the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Municipalities dealing with the fundamental problems of the infrastructure of our cities and towns and the environment. The Minister will know that there are 138 cities and towns in Ontario where sewage treatment plants do not meet environmental standards. He will also know that there are east coast cities which dump their sewage directly into the ocean. There are western cities with an incredible overflow and leakage problems in the sewage facilities. The federal Government has steadfastly refused to participate with the municipalities in meeting this problem.
Can the Minister of the Environment explain why, with all the Prime Minister's grandstanding on the environment, particularly tonight in Vancouver, the federal Government has done nothing to deal with the sewage treatment problem? Why is it that the Minister of the Environment does not want to get to the problem right at its source?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: MEETING WITH CANADIAN FEDERATION OF MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the task before us is enormous. Governments must do their share as dictated by their jurisdictions. The federal Government will do its share, and it expects other levels of government to do the same. It so happens that sewage treatment systems are a municipal and provincial matter, and that here in Canada we have a serious problem because of the fact that water is not taxed at a realistic level. If Canadian municipalities were to tax water at the same levels as their U.S. counterparts, they would have no trouble in raising the billions of dollars required to renew these systems.

subtopic: THE EFFECTS OF THE CLOSURE OF VIA RAIL ON THE ENVIRONMENT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: THE EFFECTS OF THE CLOSURE OF VIA RAIL ON THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem is not exclusively municipal or provincial, because all Canadian municipalities and all the provinces are agreed on a proposal to share the cost three ways. The Minister and his Government continue to reject these proposals.
The Minister, I imagine, must be very surprised, if I may look at his twin, the other Bouchard, without wishing to violate the Standing Orders. He must be very surprised at the words of his colleague, the Minister of Transport, who tells us that an environmental assessment review is not necessary to evaluate the impact of closing down VIA Rail passenger services.
After careful consultation with the experts and after consulting the Government's body of documentation, we found that on average, for every passenger transported over a distance of one mile, the automobile uses four times as much energy and creates four times as much pollution as the train in rural regions, and uses ten times as much energy and creates ten times as much pollution in urban areas.
Since VIA Rail produced 1.5 billion passenger-miles last year, would the Minister of the Environment agree that closing down VIA Rail will have a very negative and even disastrous impact on our country's environment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: THE EFFECTS OF THE CLOSURE OF VIA RAIL ON THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, the Government's position is that the EARP process does not put any legal obligation on the Government to assess measures that have the effect of reducing the Budget deficit. The Leader of the Opposition, himself a former Finance Minister, knows perfectly well that budgetary decisions are sovereign decisions.

June 8, 1989
Oral Questions
Regarding the deficit-reducing measure applying to our railways and its impact on the environment, Mr. Speaker, I fail to see how maintaining, at great expense-an annual deficit of $500 million-trains that criss-cross Canada empty and produce pollution can help the environment. What will help the environment is funds that will become available as result of the deficit reductions and which can then be allocated to other sectors, including the environment.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REGULATIONS TO PROTECT GREAT LAKES
REQUEST FOR REGULATIONS TO PROTECT GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. Ele is aware that the Great Lakes are becoming a massive toxic soup. The recent International Joint Commission report outlines the current and future danger. We can only guess at the health effects of the 30,000 different chemicals used there.
Two years after amending the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement, which promised programs to deal with all sources of contamination, the Government still has not followed through. Will the Minister finally support a two-pronged effort to both clean up the Great Lakes and create new, strong regulations to protect this vital national resource?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REGULATIONS TO PROTECT GREAT LAKES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is forgetting that the Government is in the process of defining 17 remedial action plans for the Great Lakes. There are 17 hot spots for which we will have remedial action plans, with funding of $125 million. This action must be seen in comparison to the $110 million plan announced today to de-pollute the St. Lawrence River. I call that action.

Mr. Speaker, since 1,000 new chemicals a year are generated around the Great Lakes and at least 500 are suspected to affect human health, will the Minister commit further funds today for the research, regulation and reduction of toxic chemicals before the crisis becomes irreversible?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this question is of great concern to the Government and all Canadians. We agree with the Opposition that we must pursue the programs we have set up to eliminate as soon as possible this high level of toxics in the Great Lakes. We have had success. We have taken drastic measures. Last year we strengthened agreements with the United States, and there will be more action.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. When the Conservatives wanted to deregulate the airlines we were told that deregulation would mean lower air fares and greater consumer choices. That was in January, 1988. Today, in June, 1989, two airlines control 98 per cent of the domestic market and effective competition has died. The author of a recent study is predicting that air fares will go up 30 per cent in the next year. What steps will the Minister of Transport take to ensure that Canadians have real competition in the air?

Mr. Speaker, first I should point out that I did not read the Roman report, so I am not in a position to comment on it.
One thing I can say though, as I pointed out yesterday with respect to the deregulation process launched by the then Minister of Transport and current Deputy Prime Minister, is that all regions of Canada now derive benefits from deregulation in the sense that a number of services which are now available were not even offered five or six years ago.
As to the fare issue, it is of course a very complex problem because depending on regions and flight types-transcontinental fares, for instance-some fares are down by as much as 80 per cent. All told, I would suggest that Canadians have benefited from deregulation.
June 8, 1989

subtopic: INCREASE IN FARES ON VIA RAIL
INCREASE IN FARES ON VIA RAIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister said he has not read the report, but he has the answers. He has not read this report, and in the last two days he admitted to our Leader that he has not read VIA's proposal on cut-backs. Does the Minister not understand that there is a place for air travel and rail travel in this country, and that by the Government's actions which is forcing VIA to increase fares, abandon routes, and reduce services, it will also destroy rail transportation in this country?

subtopic: INCREASE IN FARES ON VIA RAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we realize that that question is not about air transportation. It is always a question about VIA Rail and it means having the same answer. VIA Rail has to consider increasing fares, cutting routes and so on. VIA Rail first has to consider living within the reference levels we have given it.
Once again, we cannot afford to put as much money as the Hon. Member believes we can into empty trains.

Mr. Speaker, we are talking about transportation in this country. We have lost all forms of competition in the air. The Government is cutting back on VIA Rail.
Let me give a specific example of what it is doing in my area. The Government is forcing the same train crew on the route from Winnipeg to Churchill to stay on that train for 80 hours. That goes against all the recommendations of the Foisy report which stated that there must be well-rested crews. Not only is the Minister destroying competition, he is destroying safety. What will he do?

Mr. Speaker, one can always try to make the situation appear more critical. My colleague from Churchill knows full well that train travel and railroad beds in that region are further complicated by recurrent frost, that rail maintenance is extremely difficult, and that CN management have done everything possible to find a solution to the problem.
Oral Questions
My colleague seeks to bring up the case of the port of Churchill. Later this afternoon at 4 o'clock we will meet with a Churchill delegation to listen to what they have to say in an attempt to find answers acceptable to both sides.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. The Prime Minister of Canada is in direct disagreement with the Auditor General concerning the expenditures made under the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Development Agreement. The $20 million gift of federal taxpayers' money spent on a project not even related to the purposes of the fund in the riding of the Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is appalling.
How can the Deputy Prime Minister justify such pork-barrelling schemes when, on the other hand, this Government as a result of its recent Budget has cut back on child care spaces, has slashed ERDA funding in Atlantic Canada, and has dismissed hundreds of applications made under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency? How can the Deputy Prime Minister and the Government of Canada justify such appalling action?

people of Nova Scotia have a better life and better opportunities and the opportunity for jobs.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Prior to the recent Budget both he and the Prime Minister had repeatedly assured Canadians that the Government would not attempt to reduce its deficit at the expense of lower income earners.
However, according to a recent study based on Statistics Canada models, over half of all families with incomes of less than $25,000 a year, a total of almost two million households, will suffer a further drop in their incomes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Prior to the one o'clock adjournment, the Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) had referred to the Bill introduced into Congress by Congressman Synar. I wish to make it very clear that no Minister of the Government in any way expressed opposition to the Bill. The individual in question who phoned Congressman Synar on June 1, Mr. Ross Glasgow, who is the First Secretary of environmental matters, indicated to the Congressman Synar or his officials, or to whomever he spoke, that the Government of Canada and the Embassy in Washington had no reservations with the principle of the Bill, but did express reservations about the extra-territorial nature of the Bill. That was the difficulty the Embassy officials were
expressing. That is the only reservation about the Bill that has been expressed by anyone on behalf of the Government of Canada.

I am a little confused. The Parliamentary Secretary states that the Embassy individual involved was not acting on behalf of any Minister. It is my understanding that when the Embassy calls, and in this particular case Mr. Glasgow stated that he was calling on behalf of the Ambassador, the Ambassador is a servant of the Government and he is acting on instructions either from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) or the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard).
I do not believe that the Ambassador picks up the phone and makes calls, or asks someone to make calls in relation to a piece of legislation, without having first checked on the Government's position with his political masters. The current Ambassador knows enough about government process that I am quite sure he was fully briefed by the Minister of the Environment and the Secretary of State for External Affairs before his First Secretary placed that call.
If I am to understand the Parliamentary Secretary, the Ambassador or the Embassy is somehow acting on their own. If they are not acting on their own, on whose behalf in the Government did they call to express their concerns about the legislation? Was it the Minister of the Environment, or was it the Secretary of State for External Affairs?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
The Minister of Environment (Mr. Bouchard) indicated in the House when this issue first arose that the officials in Washington were clearly not acting on the instructions of the Minister of the Environment. He made that very clear during the discussion in the House early last week.
The point I wish to make, and the question I wish to ask, is to indicate that that official expressed support for the principle of the Bill, but expressed reservations about the extra-territorial nature of the Bill. I would like to ask the Hon. Member again whether or not that Hon. Member and the Party she represents does not also share those reservations about the extra-territorial nature of Congressman Synar's Bill?
June 8, 1989

Am I to understand that the First Secretary was acting on instructions of the Secretary of State for of External Affairs (Mr. Clark)? I am still confused. If in fact the Canadian Embassy in Washington is making calls to a congressman's office on an environmental matter without first having vetted their contact and having been briefed specifically by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard), then I maintain my original premise that the Minister of the Environment is not doing his job. Remember, this is the Minister who came into office five months ago stating that every government initiative and every project and step taken by the Government would first be cleared through the Minister of the Environment. Now we hear the Parliamentary Secretary saying that a call was made to a congressman's office with respect to a waste management Bill, and the Minister of the Environment was not involved in developing a position on that particular issue.
